Choosing an open LLM for a study used to mean trawling through leaderboards, blog posts, and model cards — and still not knowing whether the training data is public or whether the license allows research use. `openllm-selector` collects the information that actually matters for researchers into one queryable database of 18 curated models, so you can filter and compare them in a few lines of Python.

## Installation

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/Programming-The-Next-Step-2026/openllm-selector.git@week-3
```

## Researcher workflow

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A([Research question]) --> B{What constraints matter?}
    B --> C[Compute budget\nmax_size_b]
    B --> D[License\nlicense / exclude_license]
    B --> E[Training transparency\nopen_training_data\nintermediate_checkpoints]
    B --> F[Language support\nmultilingual]
    C & D & E & F --> G["filter_models()"]
    G --> H["rank_by_openness()"]
    H --> I{One clear winner?}
    I -- yes --> J["get_model() +\nfetch_recent_papers()"]
    I -- no --> K[Add more filters\nor relax constraints]
    K --> G
    J --> L([Choose model])
```

## Loading the database

```python
import openllm_selector as o

models = o.load_models()
print(f"{len(models)} models available")
#> 18 models available
```

Each record is a plain dict with 18 fields covering size, architecture, license, openness indicators, and links to the foundational paper and HuggingFace.

## Filtering

`filter_models()` accepts any combination of keyword arguments. All parameters are optional and compose with AND logic.

**Find fully open models (openness score 5):**

```python
fully_open = o.filter_models(min_openness=5)
for m in fully_open:
    print(m["name"], "—", m["license"])
#> OLMo 7B — Apache 2.0
#> OLMo 2 7B — Apache 2.0
#> Pythia 6.9B — Apache 2.0
```

**Find multilingual models under 10 B parameters with an Apache license:**

```python
results = o.filter_models(multilingual=True, license="Apache", max_size_b=10)
for m in results:
    print(m["name"], f"({m['size_b']} B)")
#> Falcon 7B (7.0 B)
#> Qwen2 7B (7.6 B)
#> Yi 1.5 9B (9.0 B)
```

**Exclude model families or countries:**

```python
# Decoder-only models, no Llama license, not from China
o.filter_models(
    architecture="decoder-only",
    exclude_license="Llama",
    exclude_country_of_origin="China",
)
```

## Ranking by openness

`rank_by_openness()` sorts any list — or the full database — by how openly a model was released (weights, training data, checkpoints, code, and license).

```python
ranked = o.rank_by_openness()
for m in ranked[:5]:
    print(f"{m['openness_score']}  {m['name']}")
#> 5  OLMo 7B
#> 5  OLMo 2 7B
#> 5  Pythia 6.9B
#> 4  BLOOM 176B
#> 4  GPT-NeoX 20B
```

Pass a pre-filtered list to rank a subset:

```python
subset = o.filter_models(family="Mistral")
o.rank_by_openness(subset, descending=False)  # least open first
```

## Searching and looking up models

`search()` does a case-insensitive substring search across name, family, and organization:

```python
o.search("eleuther")
#> [{'name': 'Pythia 6.9B', ...}, {'name': 'GPT-NeoX 20B', ...}]
```

`get_model()` retrieves a single record by exact name (case-insensitive):

```python
model = o.get_model("Pythia 6.9B")
print(model["foundational_paper"])
#> https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.01373
print(model["huggingface_id"])
#> EleutherAI/pythia-6.9b
```

## Fetching recent papers

`fetch_recent_papers()` queries the arXiv API for the most recent papers mentioning a model by name:

```python
papers = o.fetch_recent_papers("OLMo", max_results=3)
for p in papers:
    print(p["published"][:10], p["title"])
    print(" ", p["arxiv_url"])
```

This is useful for a quick literature check before committing to a model.

---

## Example: picking a model for a training-dynamics study

Suppose you are studying how in-context learning ability develops over training. You need a model with **intermediate checkpoints** (so you can probe the model at different training stages), small enough to run on a single GPU (**≤ 10 B parameters**), and with the most permissive possible openness profile.

**Step 1 — filter:**

```python
candidates = o.filter_models(
    intermediate_checkpoints=True,
    max_size_b=10,
)
for m in candidates:
    print(m["name"], f"({m['size_b']} B,  score {m['openness_score']})")
#> OLMo 7B (7.0 B,  score 5)
#> OLMo 2 7B (7.0 B,  score 5)
#> Pythia 6.9B (6.9 B,  score 5)
```

All three score 5 — the highest possible — so ranking by openness doesn't break the tie. The deciding factors are architecture and context window:

```python
for m in candidates:
    print(m["name"], "| context:", m["context_window"], "| checkpoints:", m["intermediate_checkpoints"])
#> OLMo 7B   | context: 2048 | checkpoints: True
#> OLMo 2 7B | context: 4096 | checkpoints: True
#> Pythia 6.9B | context: 2048 | checkpoints: True
```

OLMo 2 7B has the larger context window and is the newer model, making it the strongest candidate. Pythia 6.9B is the go-to choice if you specifically need the training-dynamics community's established benchmark suite.

**Step 2 — look up the paper and recent citations:**

```python
model = o.get_model("OLMo 2 7B")
print(model["foundational_paper"])
#> https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00656

papers = o.fetch_recent_papers("OLMo 2", max_results=3)
for p in papers:
    print(p["published"][:10], p["title"])
```

Within a few seconds you have the foundational reference and the most recent papers building on the model — enough to decide whether it fits your study and to start your literature review.
